units.text: The determinants and structure of happiness in different urban environments
INTRODUCTION

For a long time, the focus of urban planning had been infrastructure development, but lately, a demand for human-centred urban development has appeared (Cardoso et al., 2022).It is based on the concept of human needs, which was introduced first by Maslow, and suggests that one of the main objectives of urban planning is to create cities that make people 'richer, smarter, greener, healthier and happier' (Glaeser, 2011).In other words, one of the key areas of development becomes the well-being of residents.Well-being is widely understood as 'good mental states, including all of the various evaluations, positive and negative, that people make of their lives, and the affective reactions of people to their experiences' (OECD, 2013, p. 29).It is usually estimated by a wide range of aspects of mental state (e.g., Mulligan & Zieba, 2020).Although it is often restricted to happiness, it is a different and broader concept.However, happiness is considered one of the basic components of well-being.As one of its aspects is overall satisfaction with life, including 'all human needs, desires, and demands' (Shin & Johnson, 1978, p. 477), the idea that the happiness of individuals should be the basis of urban policy has recently gained popularity worldwide (Deeming, 2013).Therefore, it becomes relevant to explore what determines and influences happiness from various perspectives.

According to previous studies, factors with a major impact on happiness are personal, such as health, family relationships, employment, etc. (e.g., Arima, 2021;Dunlop et al., 2016;So, 2020).At the same time, many factors that are directly related to an individual's happiness are 'spatially fixed', which means that local environments can partially determine these factors and, thus, the happiness of the population (Lee et al., 2022, p. 2).In this way, the determinants of happiness can differ in different urban environments.Therefore, we decided to investigate the structures of happiness, i.e., the patterns representing relations between factors defining happiness, depending on the type of urban environment.To divide cities into types, we used an original classification of Japanese municipalities depending on the progress of problems related to the aging population, since it is one of the most urgent social issues.Indeed, the share of the world population aged 65 years or over increased from 6% in 1990 to 9% and is projected to rise to 16% by 2050 (UN, 2019, p. 1).These problems are especially crucial for Japan.After peaking in 2009, the population began to decrease, and now it is one of the few countries with a negative population change rate (Population Projections for Japan, 2022).Moreover, the share of the elderly keeps rising: it exceeded 29% of the total population for the first time in 2022 (Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2022).

Happiness in the era of population aging has been studied mainly from the perspective of the happiness of the elderly population.It was found that at the individual level, happiness declines in middle age and increases again with aging (e.g., Jin et al., 2018).However, the impact of the concentration of the elderly population as an element of the urban environment on happiness is still understudied.Moreover, the aging population is related not only to demographic changes, but also to social, cultural and territorial transformations (Shimizu et al., 2020) and can lead to a physical decline in the residential environment and housing (Park, 2012;Shimizu et al., 2021).As it is a phenomenon that any country may face in the near future, it becomes crucial to understand its impact on well-being.

Based on the above, the purpose of the research is to define the structure of happiness in Japan considering the impact of different urban environments affected by problems related to population aging.

This research could contribute to existing studies by providing a further understanding of the concept of happiness in urban planning considering the impact of not only socioeconomic and sociodemographic parameters but also differences in the urban environment.In addition, happiness is analysed mostly on the level of a country or the local level of a certain territory, such as a municipality, and the impact of urban-rural differences or differences among countries is observed.In this research, we added the sub-regional level -the level of groups of municipalities of one country united by a set of characteristics -to the analysis of the whole country.In this way, more adjusted and targeted measures to improve happiness in a specific type of place could be elaborated.Also, the experience of Japan, as one of the countries with one of the most critical levels of population aging, should be relevant for other developed countries as they face the same problems.

The paper is structured as follows.In Section 2, we analyse prior studies on the socioeconomic and sociodemographic factors of happiness, differences in happiness due to living environments, the progress of aging in Japan and problems related to urban aging.We then describe the data and methods in Section 3 and present the results of our empirical analysis in Section 4. In Section 5, we offer a summary and concluding remarks.
LITERATURE REVIEW
Socioeconomic and sociodemographic factors of happiness

For a long period, most of the studies investigating factors of happiness both worldwide and in Japan have been focused predominantly on sociodemographic (age, gender, employment, marital status and health), psychological (personality) or socioeconomic (education, individual and household income) factors.The strongest factors influencing happiness are health, marriage and having children (Deeming, 2013;Dolan et al., 2008;Dunlop et al., 2016;Goldberg et al., 2012;Lenzi & Perucca, 2018;Mulligan & Zieba, 2020).The relationship between age and happiness is non-linear and is usually characterised by a U-shaped function, which means that people are happier when they are younger and when they are older (Bernini et al., 2023;Blanchflower & Oswald, 2008;Kurokawa & Ohtake, 2013).Apart from personal attributes, some economic factors, such as job conditions, are important as well, because unemployment noticeably decreases the level of happiness (Dunlop et al., 2016;Mulligan & Zieba, 2020).The relationship with income is more complicated.Increased income has been shown to have no direct impact on individual happiness, but other factors related to income, such as perceived social status, social inequality, etc., affect the level of happiness and overall life satisfaction (Blanchflower & Oswald, 2008;Goldberg et al., 2012;Li, 2016;Singh-Manoux et al., 2005;Yamaoka, 2008).Despite the fact that these previous studies, to a large extent, give us an idea of the main determinants of happiness, they do not take into account the influence of the external environment.
Happiness in different living environments

A block of studies has analysed happiness considering regional differences or differences in the characteristics of the urban environment (Aslam & Corrado, 2012;Bernini & Tampieri, 2022;Glaeser et al., 2016;Morrison, 2021;Mouratidis & Yiannakou, 2022).Most studies consider only the differences between urban and rural areas.For example, Weckroth and Kemppainen (2021) investigated the relationship between urbanity, life satisfaction and economic development on a European scale.They found that life satisfaction was 'lower in the most urban domiciles and higher in the most rural domiciles' (Weckroth & Kemppainen, 2021, p. 220).What is more, it was confirmed that once a certain average level of more objective economic well-being has been attained, other factors start having more impact on happiness, such as subjective and social aspects (Weckroth & Kemppainen, 2021, p. 221).Another study targeting Scotland also suggests that life satisfaction is higher in rural areas because of a stronger sense of community support, social capital, higher incomes and lower unemployment (Dunlop et al., 2016).However, an important condition is that there is access to the services and other facilities in a larger area than their places of living (Dunlop et al., 2016, p. 392).Also, an analysis of structures of well-being considering aspects of the urban environment was conducted on the basis of a survey of the living environment and well-being in Japan (Tanaka et al., 2020).As a result of the analysis, all prefectures were classified into six types according to the differences in the determinants of well-being, local vitality and happiness, and the characteristics of happiness in each type were described.The most influential factors for almost all types were pride and affection toward the place of living.However, the classification was done at the prefectural level, without taking into account relevant social issues.
Happiness in Japan

A profile of happiness in Japan was constructed in a study comparing the happiness profiles of several countries (Peng et al., 2021).Health was found to be the most important factor, followed by family trust.Marital status was the third most important factor, followed by the degree of freedom in life, religious participation, community belonging, age, number of children and other factors (Peng et al., 2021, p. 58).Relative social class, relative income and use of the Internet had smaller impacts.The least important factor was the level of education.However, in another comparative study it was found that high educational accomplishments impact happiness positively in China, Japan and Korea, but not so strongly in the USA (Oshio et al., 2011).Another study about the effectiveness of municipal policies aimed at increasing happiness (Wagawa, 2021) identified 12 items interrelated with subjective well-being: work, income, health, family, child-rearing, safety, connection, education, history and culture, natural environment, living environment, and leisure time.

In another study about the subjective well-being of the residents of the Tokyo capital region (So, 2012), the impact of satisfaction with one's municipality on happiness appeared to be greater than, for instance, that of workplace relationships and satisfaction with housing.

Several papers have been based on data from the 'Livability Survey' which is the largest survey focused on living preferences in Japan and explores the subjective assessment of living conditions by residents (Daito Trust Construction Co., 2022;So, 2012So, , 2020)).They have mainly analysed the satisfaction of the Japanese population with their city or housing, but they also provide insights into the factors contributing to happiness (So, 2012).The factors most positively correlated with happiness were being female, being married and having a high level of education.In terms of self-perception, the effects of a bright future, good family relations, and good job performance were important.Satisfaction with income and social status also demonstrated a positive effect.The structure of happiness based on a multiple regression analysis of personal characteristics was presented in a report based on the 2021 ranking data (Daito Trust Construction Co., 2022).

All the studies discussed above show the distinctive features of happiness in Japan, but they consider happiness either for the whole country in general or for a selected region, like the capital region.We propose to supplement the analysis by considering the characteristics at the level of groups of municipalities, which will allow us to develop more targeted measures aimed at improving happiness.
Problems related to urban aging: classifications of Japanese municipalities

Some studies have provided an overview of problems related to population aging in Japan and have introduced classifications that can be used to address the issue.A comparative evaluation of the level of urban decline in Tokyo metropolitan areas was conducted in a study by Park (2012).Three domains of urban decline (population -society, industryeconomy, and physical environment) have been analysed, and five clusters of municipalities depending on the stage and the domain of urban decline have been identified.It was found that urban decline of every type became worse as distance from the city centre increased.The patterns of the progression of urban problems in Japan were clarified in another study (Shimizu et al., 2020).Urban problems related to the aging society were outlined based on the textual analysis of contemporary academic papers.Then, they were associated with the indicators from governmental statistics.The main problems were defined by the principal component analysis of the statistical indicators, and their long-term progression process at 5-year intervals since 2000 was shown.The irreversible progression of urban aging was defined as 'cascading'.In a subsequent study, municipalities were categorised by progressing urban aging problems (Shimizu et al., 2021).In this study, we use a modified Shimizu et al.'s (2020Shimizu et al.'s ( , 2021) ) classification system because it gives the most profound description of the issue nationwide.The system is discussed in more detail in the Methods section.
DATA, INDICATORS, AND METHODS
Data

We used data from the 'Livability Survey' (Daito Trust Construction Co., Livability Survey (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023).The survey focused on living preferences and was conducted nationwide every year from 2019 to 2023 by the Daito Trust Construction Co.This survey has the largest sample among surveys in Japan designed to find out how people feel about liveability and comfort in their place of residence.The survey sample size was 801,414 people from 1889 municipalities.The sample size for each municipality was assigned on the basis of the population ratio of each municipality, so it is proportional to their actual population.We selected data for 2020-2023 to ensure that all the indicators chosen were present in the sample.In case a participant answered in multiple years, only the record of their first appearance was used.The resulting records were treated as pooled cross-sectional data.In addition, only municipalities with more than 30 respondents were selected.Hence, the sample size was reduced to 439,757 respondents and the number of municipalities to 1079.Table 1 shows the descriptive statistics for the dataset.From the survey, we selected indicators of happiness, some sociodemographic and socioeconomic indicators, some indicators of residential satisfaction, and personal character traits.As we chose data from 2020-2023, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic must be kept in mind.Research has shown inconsistent results about the influence of the pandemic on people's well-being and happiness.Whereas some results show a decrease in happiness right after the pandemic started (Forte et al., 2020;Kanbayashi et al., 2021;Tsurume et al., 2021;Yıldırım & Güler, 2021), others indicate that there was no substantial change in the level of happiness in the longer term (Helliwell et al., 2021).
Indicators
Dependent variable: happiness

According to OECD (2013), there are three aspects of happiness: life evaluation, affect (feelings) and eudemonia (a sense of meaning and purpose in life) (OECD, 2013, p. 10).This study examines the impact of urban environments on happiness, so the life evaluation aspect is the most appropriate, as it is not a short response to anything on the one hand, and is hypothesised to have a stronger relationship with the environment than eudemonia on the other.This approach is sometimes criticised because it is relative and sensitive to cultural context and personal traits (Weckroth et al., 2015, p. 316).However, as the aim of our research is to reveal the characteristics of happiness in Japan and the differences in its determinants, we opted to investigate this concept of happiness.In the survey, the 'happiness' item is formulated as 'subjective happiness' and refers to the respondent's overall happiness in life, i.e., it is close to the overall life evaluation aspect.The response scale was a numeric 10-point scale, with 1 (unhappy) and 10 (very happy) as the endpoints without definitions of the intermediate intervals.
Independent variables

The following items were used as independent variables (Table 4): gender (dummy, reference: male), age (categorical, reference: 20-30), marital status (categorical, reference: unmarried), children (dummy, reference: no children), annual household income (categorical, reference: 0-1199 thousand yen), household assets (categorical, reference: 0-999 thousand yen), having doctoral degree (dummy, reference: no doctoral degree), unemployed (dummy, reference: employed), hours worked >60/week (dummy, reference: hours worked less than <60/week), receiving social benefits (dummy, reference: no social benefits), residential satisfaction (satisfaction with housing and with the living area, continuous, -1 for very dissatisfied to 2 for very satisfied), three indicators of self-recognition (continuous, -1 for totally disagree to 2 for totally agree), and two indicators of sense of disparity (continuous, -1 for totally disagree to 2 for totally agree).In this survey, the living area means the municipality the respondent lives in.
Methods

Our aim was to define the structure of happiness in Japan as the relations between factors defining happiness and to reveal the differences in the structures of happiness in different urban environments.To do this, we needed to select the components of the structure.Ordinal logistic regression was conducted on 31 indicators from the Livability Survey as the method most frequently used for measuring happiness as an ordered response variable, to reveal the relationship between happiness and the selected indicators.Based on the results, we chose the most powerful determinants of happiness as a basis for hypothetical models of happiness.Path analysis was used to test which hypothesised models were most concordant with the collected data.To identify the latent variables that would increase the goodness-of-fit of the model of happiness, we conducted a factor analysis with promax rotation.All of the above analyses were conducted in R (packages 'lavaan' and 'psych').

We analysed the data for all of Japan and then investigated the differences in happiness among types of municipalities, considering the problems related to urban aging.The classifications are based on modified classifications from previous research (Golubchenko et al., 2023;Shimizu et al., 2021).For this paper, three types of municipalities were selected: type II ('Population aging areas') and type III ('Low-density regional areas') where various problems related to population aging are most advanced; and type VII ('Young population and family areas'), with a high concentration of young population, especially families.In this way, we will be able to analyse the structures of happiness of problematic areas and compare them with the structure of the least problematic areas with a high potential for development.Examples of cities belonging to each type are presented in Table 2 and descriptive statistics of the respondents in Table 3.The distributions of happiness in Japanese municipalities across the entire country and by types are presented in Figure A1 in the supplemental online material.

(1) Type II ('Population aging areas') contains mostly regional municipalities with a high concentration of the elderly.Thus, they represent a worst-case scenario for the future of typical Japanese municipalities.However, the objective situation in terms of infrastructure and facilities is better than in type III cities, although they are still underdeveloped.The level of happiness in these municipalities is the second lowest.

(2) Type III ('Low-density regional areas') represents small municipalities with a high degree of population dispersion and facilities and the worst transportation accessibility.They are located primarily in northeast Japan.Besides, there is a higher number of staying population, while the population aging value is lower than in type II.The level of happiness here is also a little lower than in type II.(3) Most type VII ('Young population and family areas') municipalities are located on the outskirts of central areas.The distinguishing feature of this type is the large number of young families and a lower concentration of the elderly.Therefore, they include the most desirable demographic scenario.However, the development of facilities is surprisingly insufficient for such promising areas.Still, the level of happiness here is notably higher than in types II and III.
Based on the above, two hypotheses were formulated:

Hypothesis 1.There is a certain impact on happiness of factors characterising the place of living, although it is weaker than that of the socioeconomic, sociodemographic factors.Hypothesis 2. There are differences in the structure of happiness due to the differences in the urban environments and population structure, and they could be partly explained by the problems related to population aging.
Robustness check

As the main source is a survey, although a random sampling method was used, there are potential issues of selection bias.Particularly, many municipalities in northeastern Japan (especially, the prefectures of Hokkaido and Aomori) are not represented in the survey.Presumably, they have an insufficient sample size because of low population density.Another issue is internet access.As the survey was conducted online, the elderly population may not be widely represented.However, as we mainly aim to investigate not the happiness of the elderly, but the impact of population aging on the entire population, it may not critically influence the results.

In the ordinal logistic regression, we conducted the analysis combining 66 indicators of personal attributes, satisfaction with various aspects of life and the living area, that could potentially influence happiness based on a previous study (Daito Trust Construction Co., 2022).After comparing several models, the number of indicators was reduced to 31 according to their significance and power of influence.As for testing the coefficients for the difference, their 95% confidence intervals were checked for overlapping, and only the coefficients whose intervals do not overlap were discussed as different (Table A2 in the supplemental online material).

In the path analysis, endogeneity issues related to reverse causality, correlation with a variable that is exogenous to the model, or error terms were also considered.Indeed, some latent variables defined by factor analysis that are the strongest predictors of happiness, especially those related to self-perception ('Socioeconomic stability' or 'A sense of decline') can be influenced by subjective feelings of happiness themselves.We therefore tested path models with reverse directions of the relationship between independent and dependent variables.All of them had lower fit rates than the models selected and presented in the study.In addition, the changes in direction did not lead to significant changes in other coefficients of the models.Then, we performed Park and Gupta's Gaussian copula test, which is recommended by a range of studies on path analysis (Gui et al., 2023;Sarstedt et al., 2020).As a result, one latent variable defined by two strong predictors of happiness (marital status and having children) was excluded because of endogeneity.In the adjusted models, there are no potential correlations with error terms (Table A3 in the supplemental online material).Finally, we analysed the 95% confidence intervals (Table A4 in the supplemental online material) to check for the significance of the differences in the models.Variables related to the source of income were excluded at this stage because of a large standard error, and thus a low significance of the impact.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Determinants of happiness: entire country

For the entire territory of Japan, the impacts of 30 out of 31 chosen indicators on happiness appear to be significant (Table 4).The numbers and percentages of respondents for the ordinal logistic regression samples are presented in Table A1 in the supplemental online material.Some results fully support the findings of most of the previous research.Having a permanent partner, whether married or cohabitating, has the strongest impact on happiness (Deeming, 2013;Goldberg et al., 2012;Lenzi & Perucca, 2018).Being female also has a significant positive relationship with happiness, as well as having a doctoral degree.Although the latter result contradicts that of previous studies (Dunlop et al., 2016;Peng et al., 2021), it has been confirmed to be characteristic of Eastern Asian countries in general (Oshio, 2012).The negative impact of being middle-aged on happiness is also confirmed (Bernini et al., 2023;Blanchflower & Oswald, 2008;Dunlop et al., 2016;Kurokawa & Ohtake, 2013).

The factor related to overwork -working more than 60 h a week -predictably has a negative influence on happiness.Almost all the factors related to self-recognition indicators, except for 'Confidence in health', have a noticeable positive impact.These results are in line with previous analyses of the Livability Survey (Daito Trust Construction Co., 2022).

The larger the household income, the larger its positive impact on happiness is, especially for a very large income (more than 50 million yen per year).According to previous studies, income affects happiness indirectly by ensuring stability and access to various goods and amenities (Blanchflower & Oswald, 2008;Goldberg et al., 2012;Li, 2016;Singh-Manoux et al., 2005;Yamaoka, 2008).Therefore, the stronger impact of a large income might be associated with a higher social status.The impact of household assets on happiness varies less than that of household income, so owning assets itself might offer a greater sense of security and stability, increasing the level of happiness regardless of the amount of the assets.In addition, receiving social benefits has a positive influence on happiness.Social benefit as an additional source of income is rarely included while analysing happiness, but such a result indicates that the importance of financial support for vulnerable population groups should not be neglected.

It is worth noting that happiness is affected less by 'Satisfaction with the living area' than by 'Satisfaction with housing'.Also, both indicators of a sense of disparity negatively affect happiness.These results contradict the results based on European data, particularly from Scotland, about the absence of a relationship between inequality and life satisfaction (Dunlop et al., 2016).However, the results of a comparative study across East Asian countries, which showed that being in a self-reported low social class was strongly related to low life satisfaction are confirmed (Choia et al., 2016;Yamaoka, 2008).Some of the results differ from those of most previous research.According to previous studies, having children has a substantial impact on happiness (Deeming, 2013;Goldberg et al., 2012;Lenzi & Perucca, 2018).In our analysis, the impact is not strong, but it is still significant.Yet, in some studies, it has been found that having children could have a negative influence on the life satisfaction of parents because of additional financial and psychological pressure (Evenson & Simon, 2005;Sato, 2022).Also, health is considered to be a main determinant of happiness (Dunlop et al., 2016;Peng et al., 2021).Nevertheless, in our analysis, it appears to have a weaker relationship with happiness than most of the indicators.In addition, being unemployed surprisingly has a positive impact on happiness, which is in contrast to many previous studies (Dolan et al., 2008;Dunlop et al., 2016).It might be explained by the fact that most unemployed people in the sample had the option of not working because they had enough assets to live on.For instance, according to several studies, the highest level of life satisfaction is among non-working women without children (Sato, 2022), so, there might be the same pattern for happiness.

The values of the impact of most indicators in type II ('Population aging areas') are closest to the values of those for the entire territory of Japan.There is a stronger positive impact of the highest household income, but the difference is not statistically significant.The main difference is that having a doctoral degree affects happiness negatively, not positively, as at the level of the whole country.This may indicate the lack of conditions for the realisation of the potential of its holders and unjustified expectations of benefits associated with it.

The effects of indicators on happiness of type III ('Low-density regional areas') are also similar to those for the entire territory of Japan and type II.The main difference is that only in this type, the strong negative impact of being remarried after being widowed is significant, although the share of the elderly in these municipalities is not the highest.So, it is not possible to explain it for objective reasons.What is important, having a doctoral degree also has a negative impact, probably for the same reasons as in the previous type.

As for type VII ('Young population and family areas'), the impact of only 17 indicators appeared to be significant.Also, although there are some small differences in the impact of the variables, according to the confidence intervals these differences are not significant.In other words, the factors and their strength of influence on happiness practically do not differ from other territories.Nevertheless, the level of happiness in these municipalities is higher than in those where the problems associated with aging are most aggravated.Therefore, the influence of other factors is present, and one of them might be the characteristics of the urban environment.This issue requires further research.

In all three types, three indicators of self-recognition ('Future is bright', 'Family relations are good' and 'Work is going well') have larger values than most of the indicators.Therefore, people's subjective assessments of the social aspects of life and future prosperity appear to be more important for happiness than most of those related to socioeconomic and demographic factors.Furthermore, the living environment has a notable impact on happiness through satisfaction with the living area, especially with one's own housing.
Structure of happiness: path analysis

On the basis of the results of the regression analysis, we selected eight variables for path analysis, all of which have a significant impact on happiness and were included in all models: 'Female', 'Satisfaction with home', 'Satisfaction with the living area', 'Future is bright', 'Family relations are good', 'Work is going well', 'Feeling like a lower social class' and 'Inferior in income & social status'.With the help of the factor analysis, we determined three factors as latent variables, which coincide in all types.Factor 1 ('Socioeconomic stability') is defined by indicators related to expectations for the future, family relations and work.Factor 2 ('A sense of decline') is characterised by perceiving oneself as a lower social class and having an overall sense of insecurity in one's social and economic situation.Factor 3 ('Residential satisfaction') represents the two indicators of satisfaction with the place of living: satisfaction with housing and with the wider residential areathe municipality.

One variable -'Female' -affects happiness through a direct path (i.e., it is not included in the three factors but is included in the models).The relationship between happiness and each of the variables in the path analysis is significant (p < 0.05).The models of happiness for each type with the best fits are presented in Figures 1-4.

In the model of happiness for Japan (Figure 1), 'Socioeconomic stability', which is directly related to subjective feelings and assessments, has the strongest positive causal relationship with happiness.'A sense of decline' has a negative causal relationship with happiness.What is important, the factor 'Residential satisfaction' which is defined by the satisfaction with both the immediate and wider living environment also contributes to happiness.So, the hypothesis that it affects happiness was confirmed.

Moreover, there is no significant difference in the structures of models (Figures 2-4) in the types revealed.Thus, if we analyse what components define the happiness of the population of each type in general, there is no significant difference neither in the components nor in their   Stanislava Golubchenko et al.

CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK

This analysis examined the relationship between happiness and selected indicators from the 'Livability Survey' related to sociodemographic and socioeconomic parameters, residential satisfaction, self-recognition and sense of disparity, as well as the differences in these relationships depending on the type of urban environment.We also evaluated the structures of happiness in all of Japan and the selected types.

We found that indicators that are related to subjective personal assessments of social stability and future aspirations influence happiness more than most socioeconomic and demographic indicators.Moreover, it was confirmed that satisfaction with the place of living has a significant positive impact on happiness, even if it is included in the model together with personal factors.Some differences in the determinants of happiness in the selected types were observed.

We also described the structure of happiness, which was composed of three factors ('Socioeconomic stability', 'A sense of decline' and 'Residential satisfaction') in all types.The strongest impact of the factor directly related to subjective feelings and assessments of the social aspects of life was confirmed in all of the types.However, no significant differences in the structures were revealed.
Based on the results, as well as some other characteristics of the types of municipalities, it is possible to make recommendations aimed at raising the level of happiness in the local population.

The tools of territorial development are very diverse.The most common are economic measures, which can be direct (e.g., loans and subsidies) and indirect (e.g., tax benefits).There are also administrative ways to support cities and regions: strategic planning documents and regulations, or verbal orders from the authorities.In addition, there is a variety of social engineering techniques.It was confirmed in several studies that a mix of policy instruments over time has a greater impact, relative to receiving a single policy instrument or static instrument mix (Cunningham et al., 2016, p. 527;Lenihan et al., 2023).All regional policy measures can be attributed to one or more of the spheres of social life: economy and technological development (including the information sphere), society, ecology, culture, politics and security.One of the examples of technological policy is R&D (e.g., R&D grants, R&D tax credits and publicly supported academic-industry collaborations) (Lenihan et al., 2023, p. 768).As for the adaptation of policy measures aimed at improving happiness, it is important that although they may have much in common in many countries, they will still differ by certain unique policy instruments or their coordination, due to the characteristics of every country (Lenihan et al., 2020).However, the major essential common feature is that 'it may be the sequencing of instruments over time that is of key importance, rather than the actual interplay of instruments at a given phase' (Cunningham & Link, 2021;Cunningham et al., 2016, p. 527).Thus, adaptation and consistency are two especially important points.

The model of happiness of type II ('Population aging areas') is very similar to the model of the entire country.Considering that these areas have a greater than average aging population concentration, this can be considered good, as its overall effect on happiness appeared to be less than might be expected.These areas will need support to prevent conditions from deteriorating.For this purpose, standard measures to support the aging population, such as advanced development of social security, health care (including telemedicine), clubs for the elderly and remote forms of employment should be helpful.

In type III ('Low-density regional areas'), there is a relatively strong negative impact on the level of remarriage after widowhood.Accordingly, it is possible to propose general measures targeted at this specific population group: the socialisation of widows and widowers, and the creation of platforms for their psychological rehabilitation.

Types II and III, which are both characterised by not a very favourable economic situation, have one common feature -the negative impact of having a doctoral degree.This may mean the lack of conditions for the realisation of the potential of PhD holders (Araki, 2022) and, as a consequence, their dissatisfaction with their socioeconomic status.This shows the unused potential for accelerating measures in the field of R&D in these areas.For instance, even municipalities with small, but their own application centres and personnel -locations of laboratories, universities and research centres -can use them as bases for technological development (e.g., Zentsūji-shi and Tōon-shi from type II, or Nishihara-chō from type III).The creation of a system of personnel reserve, platforms for scientists to communicate with each other, strengthening of foundations-grantors, etc. might also be useful.

Interestingly, although the level of happiness in type VII ('Young population and family areas') is higher than in the other two types, there are no significant differences in their models.Therefore, the higher happiness might be explained by two distinguishing features of this type: a relatively young population and a location closer to developed centres.Given the shortcomings in the development of the infrastructure in these types of municipalities, which was considered in a previous study (Golubchenko et al., 2023), it is possible to increase the level of happiness in these areas, considering their characteristics.It is important to stimulate the realisation of youth initiatives, to provide the increased need for a variety of leisure activities.Considering the location of these municipalities on the outskirts of developed centres, this could be done, primarily, through the branches of relevant firms and the public sector.

In sum, although this study makes a clear contribution to our understanding of the determinants and structure of happiness both in Japan and in the selected types, certain important questions remain unanswered, suggesting possibilities for future research.First, considering the large number of indicators used, a more detailed study to define the determinants of happiness and relationships could be conducted.This would enable us to clarify the relationships between the indicators or blocks of indicators.Secondly, we did not analyse the results for all of the types from the suggested classification.Additional comparisons with other types or by using a typology of different social problems would allow researchers to elaborate on other place-based and targeted measures aimed at increasing happiness.Finally, it would be useful to conduct a similar analysis of the determinants and structure of happiness by different population groups, rather than by municipality types.
